note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea; no clear food or environmental trigger identified. Brother experienced similar illness 5 days ago → likely infectious exposure.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Onset Monday/Tuesday (≈3 days ago); diarrhoea hourly when awake; not improving.
- ENT symptoms: 
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation – denied/not reported.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness – one brief mention by clinician; patient did not confirm (“conflict noted”).  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnoea, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, ear/neck symptoms – none reported.
- Other gastrointestinal symptoms: lower-mid abdominal cramp preceding stools (≈6/10), occasional vomiting (worse with milk), feels febrile (temperature not measured), reduced urine frequency; denies blood per rectum.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: Brother currently recovering from similar illness; patient no prior similar episodes; no ED visits/injections.
- Allergies and current medications: No known drug/food allergies. Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) for pain/fever.
- Social context: Lives with mother and sister; brother lives elsewhere. Works in a central London government office. Occasional social smoker; alcohol socially 1–2×/month.

Objective:
- Observable swelling (lips, tongue, uvula, face): Not observed/not reported.
- Airway/breathing: No stridor, wheeze, or dyspnoea reported.
- Mental status: Alert and conversant on video call.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Others present with patient during call: Not stated.

Assessment:
- Likely acute infectious gastroenteritis with risk of dehydration.
- No current evidence of ENT or airway involvement. Brief mention of “feeling hoarse” not corroborated by patient (conflict noted).

Plan:
- Oral rehydration: Advise purchasing over-the-counter Dioralyte; take as directed to replace fluids/electrolytes.
- Diet: Clear fluids initially (water, oral rehydration solution); progress to soft foods (soups, mashed foods) as tolerated.
- Medications: Continue Paracetamol for abdominal cramps/fever (avoid excess alcohol).
- Monitoring/Red flags: If symptoms persist >48 hours, worsen, signs of dehydration (dizziness, reduced urine, inability to keep fluids), high fever, or any new airway/ENT symptoms (voice change, throat tightening, breathing difficulty), patient to call back or seek emergency care.
- Follow-up: Telephone review if no improvement in 1–2 days; consider further investigations and possible stool studies or IV fluids if deteriorating.
- Education: Avoid alcohol while unwell; maintain hand hygiene to reduce household transmission.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: No vital signs, physical abdominal exam, or ENT exam documented; no formal allergy list beyond “none known”; hydration status (mucous membranes, capillary refill) not assessed; stool characteristics (colour/odor) not documented.
● Internal conflicts: Clinician stated patient “feeling hoarse,” patient did not endorse—conflict noted.
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional minor interruptions but overall adequate for documentation.
